title: Vertical Integration Becoming Pervasive
gist: Hardware/software co-design is being revived after failing 30 years ago, but with the causality inverted: software now iterates faster than silicon, so hardware development is playing catch-up to workloads rather than the reverse. Energy and thermal density — batteries at the edge, power density in AI data centers — are the forcing function pushing companies toward specialized silicon even amid rapid change, with RISC-V custom extensions, matrix-extension proliferation, and multiphysics-aware EDA tooling as the visible manifestations, and a missing software-to-power dataset blocking AI from automating the problem.

insights.claim: Hardware/software co-design was attempted thirty years ago and failed because the technology was inadequate, driving the industry toward assembling pre-verified IP blocks instead of top-down partitioning — a path dependency that still shapes today's design flows.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: The IP-assembly business model exists because co-design failed; if co-design now succeeds, IP vendors' packaging of value must change.
insights.quote: The industry went in the direction of using assemblies of pre-verified IP blocks, which were integrated together rather than a top-down design flow based on partitioning.
insights.locator: Thirty years ago, there was a lot of interest

insights.claim: Surviving co-design technology — virtual prototypes plus untimed and approximately timed SystemC models — is still not considered an adequate solution for the realistic workloads encountered today, leaving a genuine tooling gap.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: An acknowledged capability gap in a market with urgent demand is where new EDA revenue and startup formation appear.
insights.quote: Today, those virtual prototypes encompass many more engines, but they are still not viewed as being an adequate solution for realistic workloads encountered today.
insights.locator: Much of the technology developed at that time

insights.claim: In the past decade virtual prototyping has extended into virtual twin modeling, which incorporates physical inputs and sensor interfaces rather than modeling only compute.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Virtual twin modeling expands EDA's addressable scope from chip into system and physical environment — a TAM extension for simulation vendors.
insights.quote: In the past decade, virtual prototyping has extended to modeling of physical inputs and sensor interfaces in what is known as virtual twin modeling.
insights.locator: This has extended into more areas today

insights.claim: The historical relationship where software was relatively fixed and hardware was optimized around it has inverted: software iteration is now much faster than hardware, turning co-design into a catch-up game for silicon teams.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Hardware roadmaps chasing a faster-moving software target implies more re-spins, shorter product lives, and higher value on programmable/flexible silicon.
insights.quote: At the same time, software iteration time is now much faster than hardware, making co-design a catch-up game for hardware.
insights.locator: Today’s systems are massive compared

insights.claim: The abstraction layers historically built between software and hardware stacks for developer efficiency and reliability are now being deliberately broken open to squeeze optimization out of every part of the toolchain for performance-sensitive AI workloads.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Collapsing abstractions favors vertically integrated players who own both sides of the stack and disadvantages firms selling only one layer.
insights.quote: What we have seen change is the need to squeeze optimization out of every part of the tool chain, particularly for highly performance-sensitive workloads like AI.
insights.locator: Historically, we have constructed abstraction layers

insights.claim: A fundamental organizational divide persists between software and hardware teams working with separate tools and design flows, and this divide — not the underlying technology — is now the binding constraint on co-design.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Organizational rather than technical bottlenecks resolve slowly; discount timelines for co-design tool adoption accordingly.
insights.quote: There is a fundamental divide that exists, and it needs to change.
insights.locator: We remain a long way from that ultimate goal

themes.theme: Makimoto's Wave and the specialization swing

insights.claim: Makimoto's Wave — Tsugio Makimoto's 1990s observation that the industry oscillates between specialization and generalization — still holds, but now runs asynchronously across fragmented sectors rather than as one industry-wide cycle.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Sector-asynchronous waves mean specialization opportunities appear in one market while another consolidates — a rotation framework rather than a market-wide call.
insights.quote: Back in the 1990s, Tsugio Makimoto, then CTO at Sony, made an observation about how the industry appeared to go in waves between specialize and generalize.
insights.locator: Makimoto’s Wave

insights.claim: The industry went from an ASIC for every little thing 25 years ago, to collapsing down to just a few general-purpose architectures, and is now back to purpose-driven specific silicon with design phases overlapping rather than running serially.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: A return to per-application ASICs multiplies design starts, benefiting EDA, IP, and specialty foundry capacity more than unit volume alone would suggest.
insights.quote: Twenty-five years ago, there was an ASIC for every little thing
insights.locator: Makimoto’s Wave

insights.claim: Specialization pressure originated at the edge, where processors suddenly needed far more compute within battery power envelopes, and has since spread into data centers where power density restricts what is possible in AI.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: The same energy constraint now drives both edge and data-center silicon design, unifying the demand case for efficiency-oriented IP across markets.
insights.quote: This focus on power has spread to data centers, where thermal has become a major concern, but here it is about power densities restricting what is possible in AI.
insights.locator: Makimoto’s Wave

insights.claim: There is increasing evidence that GPUs are not the end of the story, and future data centers will be heterogeneous, full of many different ASICs, with workloads compiled to the appropriate chip inside the facility.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to GPU-centric data-center assumptions; if right, compiler/runtime layers that target heterogeneous silicon become a strategic control point.
insights.quote: There’s increasing evidence that they aren’t, and the world is going to be full of ASICs.
insights.locator: Data centers used to be packed with x86 processors

insights.claim: The economic rule governing the specialize/generalize pendulum is simple: stable software invites cost reduction through commoditization, while rapidly evolving software demands hardware innovation to keep up.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Use software stability as the leading indicator for whether a compute segment is about to commoditize or fragment into custom silicon.
insights.quote: When software becomes stable, economics attempts to drive down costs, but when software evolves rapidly, it calls for more innovation in hardware to keep up.
insights.locator: When software becomes stable

insights.claim: Hyperscalers' primary motivation for building their own chips and accelerators is co-optimization of KPIs — and the balance may be shifting from time-to-market toward power and performance as the dominant criteria.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: If hyperscalers now prioritize power/performance over speed-to-market, custom silicon programs get longer runway and merchant accelerators lose their speed advantage.
insights.quote: one of the main reasons for them to build their own chips and their own accelerators is for co-optimization of KPIs
insights.locator: When software becomes stable

themes.theme: RISC-V and the economics of custom extensions

insights.claim: RISC-V International frames the current period as the era of workload-designed silicon, with companies optimizing silicon specifically around the workload it targets.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Workload-first design is the structural driver behind RISC-V adoption — the architecture's value is customizability, not license cost alone.
insights.quote: We are in the era of workload-designed silicon.
insights.locator: Some of the changes can best be seen by looking at RISC-V

insights.claim: A miniature specialize-then-standardize wave runs inside RISC-V itself: firms build proprietary extensions and toolchains for fast innovation, then propose them as standards once the benefit no longer covers tool maintenance cost, shifting the cost of ownership onto the whole ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Predicts which proprietary RISC-V features become standards and when — a timing model for open-source ecosystem consolidation.
insights.quote: When you use the vendor or custom op codes, you own the complete cost of ownership
insights.locator: But when you dig into the surrounding ecosystem

insights.claim: RISC-V did not invent workload-tailored processors — Tensilica automated custom core and toolset creation fifteen years earlier, and RISC-V's contribution was making that concept non-proprietary.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Deflates the RISC-V technical-novelty narrative; its moat is licensing model and ecosystem openness, which is a weaker and more contestable advantage.
insights.quote: RISC-V didn’t invent the idea of tailoring a processor to a target workload.
insights.locator: When you know the workloads

insights.claim: IP companies are now designing hardware around specific customer workloads and application focus, and this workload orientation is how RISC-V architectures find differentiation in application spaces.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: IP differentiation shifts from PPA benchmarks to workload fit, which favors vendors with deep application-domain knowledge over generic core suppliers.
insights.quote: IP companies are focusing on making sure they are designing hardware around customer workloads and application focus
insights.locator: A significant overlap between the needs

insights.claim: For arbitrary software where workload insight is unavailable, generic compute engines — vector and matrix machines — must be built generically and scalably enough to deliver good-enough performance even on unpredictable AI-generated code.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Defines the boundary of specialization: unknown workloads still require general engines, so the ASIC wave does not fully displace programmable compute.
insights.quote: built generically, and scalable enough that they can have good-enough performance on an arbitrary workload, even if it’s garbled slop from AI
insights.locator: In between, there is a mix of both

insights.claim: RISC-V is running three parallel working groups on three different matrix extensions on the explicit belief that one matrix extension cannot fit all use cases, ranging from a tiny extension over existing vector registers to a full matrix register file with dedicated accumulators.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Standards fragmentation inside RISC-V raises software portability risk and toolchain cost — a real friction against the 'RISC-V takes over' thesis.
insights.quote: We have three working groups in parallel on three different options, because we believe that one matrix extension doesn’t fit all.
insights.locator: Until AI-driven co-design is ready

insights.claim: The intuitive mapping of matrix accelerator size to device class is inverted: edge AI chipsets with few cores are better served by one large shared matrix accelerator, while mass-replicated core designs favor a small matrix capability inside each core.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive sizing logic means IP vendors selling 'edge = small' product ladders may be mismatched to actual customer architectures.
insights.quote: Initially I thought the small one was for IoT devices and the full-blown matrix accelerator was for supercomputers. Then the experts start telling me, it may even be the opposite.
insights.locator: Until AI-driven co-design is ready

insights.claim: Adding many matrix registers, operations, and accumulators to a core increases both die size and power consumption, so the highest-throughput matrix option carries a direct area and energy penalty that constrains where it can be deployed.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: The area/power cost of matrix hardware is the real gating factor on AI capability at the edge — a constraint on edge-AI penetration forecasts.
insights.quote: When you start adding that many registers for matrix, die size and power consumption increase.
insights.locator: Until AI-driven co-design is ready

insights.claim: Energy is the common theme pushing everyone toward co-design — battery life at the edge and heat management in data centers are the same constraint expressed in different form factors.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: One unified driver across two markets means efficiency-focused tools and IP have a broader addressable base than either market alone.
insights.quote: A common theme pushing everyone toward co-design is energy.
insights.locator: Energy and thermal

insights.claim: Despite rhetoric about power being paramount, power remains roughly step three in the development journey — after functional correctness and timing — and software engineers lack tools to understand it early enough to act.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Power is not yet a first-order design constraint in practice, so claimed efficiency gains from co-design are further out than marketing implies.
insights.quote: But power is probably step three on the journey of getting something out into market.
insights.locator: Energy and thermal

insights.claim: A software engineer writing purely for performance without visibility into power is treated as a defect in the development process, prompting IP vendors to build tooling that surfaces power numbers to software teams during development.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Power-aware software tooling is an emerging product category attached to IP sales — watch for it as a differentiator in core licensing deals.
insights.quote: If a software engineer is writing things purely for performance and does not know what power is, that is a problem
insights.locator: That needs to change

insights.claim: The target metric for AI hardware is shifting from raw TOPS to TOPS per watt, changing how processors are specified and marketed.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Benchmark redefinition reshuffles competitive rankings — vendors leading on raw TOPS may lose position on efficiency-normalized comparisons.
insights.quote: We need to make sure we are providing targeted hardware that’s optimizing for things like TOPS per watt instead of raw TOPS.
insights.locator: That needs to change

insights.claim: Understanding performance and power in heterogeneous applications with multi-level caching may never be fully achievable, which is precisely why it remains ripe territory for new EDA tooling.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: An unsolvable-in-principle problem generates recurring tool spend rather than a one-time fix — attractive economics for EDA vendors.
insights.quote: It is possible they will never fully understand it, but that’s where power/performance tradeoffs happen.
insights.locator: Understanding performance and power is far from trivial

themes.theme: Multiphysics, tooling gaps, and the missing dataset

insights.claim: The complexity now addressable by new tooling extends well beyond hardware and software into mechanical, electromagnetic, and multiphysics domains, with the combined hardware-software unit becoming the object to which thermal and IR-drop analysis attaches.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Multiphysics attach expands EDA seat value per design and rewards vendors with both implementation and simulation portfolios.
insights.quote: You may find hardware and software engineers uniting because they now have to deal with those pesky mechanical and electromagnetic and multiphysics guys taking software, taking hardware on the chip, and now looking at thermal.
insights.locator: The problem continues to get tougher

insights.claim: Software activity data can be used to narrow which parts of a chip require deeper IR-drop investigation during a long workload, making software traces an input to physical design closure rather than just a verification artifact.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Workload-driven physical analysis is a concrete co-design mechanism that is already deployable — a near-term EDA product hook, not a research idea.
insights.quote: being able to grasp in a long workload, based on all the activity data created by software, which parts of the chip I need to look further for IR drop aspects and things like that
insights.locator: The problem continues to get tougher

insights.claim: Workload-driven power and performance analysis must extend beyond software workloads to functions like DFT, which is still a workload with its own power and performance behavior that must be factored into hardware design.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Test-mode power is an often-ignored constraint that becomes material at high densities — a niche where test/DFT tool vendors gain relevance.
insights.quote: It’s still a workload, but it includes areas like DFT, understanding from a DFT context power and performance, and what happens there.
insights.locator: To make life a little more complicated

insights.claim: LLMs cannot yet become power-aware because the training corpus does not exist: there is no dataset recording which software ran and how much power it consumed at the chip, rack, box, car, or data-center level.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: The missing software-to-power dataset is the specific bottleneck to AI-driven co-design — whoever assembles that corpus owns a defensible position.
insights.quote: Where is the data set for this software that ran and consumed this much power, whether it’s at the chip level, the server rack level, the box level, the car level, the data center level?
insights.locator: Some people have suggested that AI itself

insights.claim: Customer specifications are becoming so complicated that customers sometimes cannot articulate what they want, pushing IP vendors away from a pure off-the-shelf model toward co-development with leading-edge customers who fund new features.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: IP business models are shifting toward services-like co-development, which lowers gross margin but improves customer lock-in and roadmap intelligence.
insights.quote: Sometimes, the customer may not be able to even articulate what they want, because they want everything in the world.
insights.locator: The challenge is determining how much customization

insights.claim: The old model of adding accelerators here and there to make software run better is being replaced by asking what the software is doing and how to partition and deploy it across different elements in the system — a fundamental inversion of the hardware design question.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Partitioning-first design elevates system architects and architecture-exploration tools above block-level IP selection in the value chain.
insights.quote: Now it becomes, ‘What is the software doing, and how do we partition and deploy this on different elements in the system?'
insights.locator: Still, each time the pendulum swings

insights.claim: Architecture must be understood as three overlapping layers — macro-level hardware architecture, micro-architecture down to individual instructions, and software architecture — and system-level tools struggle across all three even as individual processor design has advanced.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: The tooling gap is at system level, not block level — a specific place where EDA incumbents are vulnerable to new entrants.
insights.quote: Architecture is overloaded in that it includes both the macro-level hardware architecture, and the micro-architecture, really understanding the instructions and how certain instructions might help.
insights.locator: While significant progress has been made

insights.claim: The era of hardware teams building something and throwing it over the wall to embedded software teams died more than two decades ago, so today's co-design discussion is about depth of integration rather than whether integration happens at all.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Sets the baseline: incremental co-design claims must be judged against two decades of existing practice, not against a strawman of total separation.
insights.quote: Long gone are the days of a hardware team building something then throwing it over the wall to an embedded software team
insights.locator: This has extended into more areas today
